body:
When we look at the sleek mechanical keyboards dominating modern desk setups, it is easy to forget that the underlying technology is rooted in over a century of mechanical engineering. The journey began with heavy-duty mechanical typewriters, where every keypress had to generate enough physical force to strike an inked ribbon against paper.

The Mechanical Era and IBM's Legacy

As computing entered the mainstream in the late 20th century, early computer terminals adopted similar heavy mechanical principles. The breakthrough came with the IBM Model M in 1985, which popularized the buckling spring mechanism. This design provided a distinct tactile bump and an audible click, ensuring typists received immediate physical confirmation that a keystroke was registered.

The Rise of Cherry MX and Modern Customization

While buckling springs ruled early enterprise offices, the German manufacturer Cherry Corporation shifted the paradigm with the introduction of the Cherry MX switch series in the 1980s. Originally classified by color-coded stems denoting actuation force and tactile feedback—Black, Blue, Brown, and Red—these switches became the gold standard for durability and reliability.

Today, the mechanical keyboard market has expanded far beyond standard office equipment into a thriving enthusiast culture. Lubrication, gasket mounts, and custom-tuned dampening materials have transformed the humble keyboard from a utilitarian peripheral into a core component of workspace ergonomics and personal expression.

title: From Clack to Comfort: The Fascinating History of Ergonomic Keyboards
summary: Discover how the typewriter's linear design forced decades of wrist strain, and how visionary engineers reshaped the modern workspace.

Highlights the anatomical breakthroughs in carpal tunnel prevention

body:
When Christopher Latham Sholes patented the QWERTY typewriter layout in the late 19th century, his primary design constraint was preventing mechanical key jams—not preserving human joint health. For over a century, typists were forced to align their wrists in an unnatural, pronated position, straight parallel to the desk edge, leading to an epidemic of carpal tunnel syndrome.

The Split Design Revolution

The journey toward ergonomic relief began in earnest during the late 20th century as computing became ubiquitous in office environments. Inventors realized that forcing human hands to angle inward at 45 to 90 degrees created chronic tension in the forearms and wrists. Early prototypes introduced the 'split' concept, physically dividing the keyboard into two independent halves that could align with the natural shoulder width of the user.

Modern Iterations

Today's ergonomic keyboards combine historical lessons with modern engineering, featuring tenting (tilting the inner edges upward), thumb clusters, and ortholinear layouts. By examining where we started, workspace designers can better optimize their desks for long-term physical well-being.
